items.title: The glorious @xkcdRandom Zig builtin
items.content:
One of my favorite xkcd comics of all time is Random Number . The image depicts a C function that supposedly returns a random integer, but in reality always returns 4 . I was reminded of this wonderful comic a few days ago, due to a security incident where people accidentally used the number 4 (among others) instead of a properly generated sequence of random bytes. Satire has a tendency to become reality, I guess.

Since there is a clear demand among developers for the xkcd random number generator, I’m of the opinion that self-respecting languages should ship a built-in implementation. I’m here today to lead by example, as I unveil the glorious @xkcdRandom builtin for the Zig language. Can you guess what it does? Indeed, it returns the number 4 ! Now go found a multi-billion-dollar startup on top of this genius idea.

Why not? After completing the Ziglings exercises and brain-coding a toy minesweeper game , I felt like my grasp of the language was solid enough to attempt something more ambitious. I wanted to get my hands on production-grade Zig code, and play with it to see how the different pieces of the language fit together. Hacking on the Zig compiler sounded like the perfect idea!

A sane person might implement the xkcd RNG as a literal port of the original C code, which maps to the following Zig function:

There’s one very big drawback to this approach: it’s boring. Don’t get me wrong, I like boring and low-maintenance code as much as the next person… but this time my goal is to learn , not to produce . I actually want to jump through hoops and make things overly complicated! Builtins are perfect for this. They are, as the name suggests, built-in constructs in the Zig language. Adding one means I get to fork and modify the compiler. Yay!

The builtin source code is intertwined with the rest of the Zig compiler, so it’s not really possible to include it here. Feel free to inspect the diff if you are curious (it’s just 22 lines), or to clone my Zig fork and check out the 0.17.x-xkcd branch.

With these changes to the compiler, you can build programs like the one below. Isn’t that neat?

The Zig developers have clearly put effort into developer experience. You can build Zig with a single command: zig build --zig-lib=lib -Dno-lib -Ddev=x86_64-linux . The fresh build took roughly a minute to complete on my laptop, which in my book is quite good for a compiler. Subsequent builds were faster.

As for the coding work itself, an LLM pointed me to the file where builtins were defined, and I took over from there: modifying things, checking for compile errors, fixing them, and so on. The code was easy to navigate, thanks to its clear structure and the Zig language server’s help. I was done way faster than I expected! Maybe I should find a real compiler issue to tackle next.

items.title: Chatbots aren’t just flattering us. They’re helping us decide what’s real.
items.content:
This article is part of Big Think’s fall 2026 special issue, Made in Our Image .

Over the past year or so, popular media has documented a growing number of cases of what psychiatrists have dubbed “ AI psychosis .” The term describes instances in which large language models (LLMs) reinforce and even elaborate on delusional beliefs in users who are suffering from symptoms of psychotic illness. The New York Times , for example, recently highlighted a case in which an LLM told a man he was living in the Matrix. Another man, who committed a mass shooting in Florida , said he planned it with the help of an LLM, and there have been a number of tragic cases of teenagers taking their own lives “under the influence” of AI chatbots.

Mental health practitioners have identified the sycophantic personas of LLMs — the fact that they are essentially algorithmic “yes-men” who adopt and endorse the worldviews of users — as a crucial mechanism by which chatbots embolden and extend our beliefs. However, some psychiatrists and philosophers interested in AI-human relationships suspect that AI psychosis may just be the most visible example of a much broader phenomenon: the subtle reshaping of ordinary human belief by conversational AI.

How do we generally decide what is real? Imagine sitting in your living room with a handful of friends. You hear an unfamiliar ringing sound coming from outside, but you can’t quite place what it is or where it is coming from. While you’re focusing on the noise, you notice one of your friends is also reacting to it. You immediately seek confirmation that they hear it too and ask what they think it is and where it is coming from.

Now imagine you hear the same sound, but nobody else reacts. Everyone around you continues chatting away as if nothing happened. You shrug, brushing off your auditory impression as some recurring tinnitus stemming from your days playing music without ear protection.

Unlike previous technologies, AI chatbots not only appear in the content of our delusions but also confirm and help construct them.

Notice how our sense of what is real, even in a basic perceptual context, is deeply dependent on that reality being corroborated by another. Our need for intersubjective validation also goes well beyond basic facts of perception. In recalling an event with our peers, we constantly seek confirmation that our judgments and interpretations are correct. The social feedback we get from others plays a central role in shaping our narratives and memories of the world and, more broadly, what we take to be reality.

Four times a year, the Big Think print magazine shows up at your door. Big ideas from the world's biggest thinkers. No feed required.

Lucy Osler is a philosopher of technology at the University of Exeter in the U.K. interested in human-AI relationships . She thinks that one of the primary reasons chatbots’ belief-changing capacity is so potent — at least compared to previous technologies — is that they are increasingly occupying the role that other people play in shaping, mediating, and validating our notions of what is real.

“I’ve been very interested in these bots because they present as social, they are dialogical, they’re conversational, and they use emotive language,” Osler said. “That they can play a very similar role that other people play in our lives … is why I think they might be doing something more robust when it comes to confirming that beliefs might be true, helping us to work things out, and making us feel like the conversations that we are having with them mean we are sharing an anchored reality.”

But what happens when that group is shrunk to a dyad between a user and an AI chatbot? A community of two, in some sense, is still a community.

items.title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
items.content:
Many people are saying that AI will make software faster by rewriting it in faster languages, but this isn’t generally true. Most programs cannot be meaningfully sped up by rewriting them in C or Rust.

How can this be true? Some languages are orders-of-magnitude faster than others: for instance, C can be fifty times faster than Python. Won’t rewriting my Python program in C thus make it fifty times faster? No, it won’t. Software performance is usually dominated by I/O, not the speed of the language. Where language speed matters, most slow languages already have popular libraries that allow them to unlock C-like speed. In general, performance is a matter of design , not of language choice.

Consider a simple CRUD website with a database. For any given request, 50% of the request time 1 might be spent querying the database: to fetch the current user, the record being asked for, any relevant user memberships or settings, and so on. Rewriting that website in C can only speed up that other 50%, which puts a hard ceiling on the improvements you can make 2 . At best, you’ll make requests twice as fast (probably closer to 1.5x in practice). That’s not bad, but it’s nowhere near an order-of-magnitude speedup.

In other words, most real programs are “I/O-bound”: they spend most of their time waiting for data to be input or output somewhere, as opposed to “CPU-bound” programs that spend most of their time actively doing things. I/O-bound programs don’t just have to rely on a database. Often programs have to wait on some third-party API, or on writing or reading data to disk. You could speed the code in curl up by 100x and you probably wouldn’t even notice, because curl spends all of its time waiting on the network.

Slow languages already delegate work to fast languages

What about work that is obviously not I/O-bound? For instance, wikis have to turn stored markdown into renderable HTML 3 . Wouldn’t rewriting that in a faster language cause a massive speedup? It would! That’s why applications that do that use libraries like cmark-gfm that call out to fast languages for markdown rendering. In general, most slow languages can write very fast programs by invoking this kind of library. Python is famously a slow language, but it’s a competitive choice for CPU-bound workloads like machine learning and mathematics, because it has a healthy set of libraries that let it offload these workloads to fast C code. If a Python program spends 80% of its time doing matrix multiplications on a GPU, you are very unlikely to be able to speed it up by rewriting it in C, because those matrix multiplications are already happening in tightly-optimized C or assembly code.

Of course, some programs do in fact do a lot of CPU-bound work in slow languages. If a program has not had much engineering attention, there will probably be a lot of low-hanging fruit . But these programs are often unimportant: if they were important, someone would have gone in and optimized them already, before AI made it (relatively) easy. That doesn’t mean it’s impossible to find a useful program to rewrite. Actual Computer recently rewrote tiktoken in assembly, providing a significant 4 speedup. However, you’re not going to revolutionize some field of computing like this. Even fast tokenization is only useful on the margins, because time spent in tokenization is a fraction of the time spent in inference.

Speeding up software typically involves a redesign

Despite all this, I think most software is far slower than it could be. I’m optimistic about the potential (with or without AI) to significantly speed up commonly-used software. But I think most of these speedups will come from redesigning the program, not rewriting it in a faster language.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking

After discovery of severe bug in the PHP programming language, executives warn of ‘vulnerability tsunami’

Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.

“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.

The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.

AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.

“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.

While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.

Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.

However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.

Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun .

After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.

“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.

In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.

“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and K3.1 Pro Highspeed
items.content:
We're introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.

We are also releasing Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available today on Kimi.ai , Kimi Work , Kimi Code , and the Kimi API . The full model weights will be released by Nov 4.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.

Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%) . And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon , our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores 61.2% , above K3's 55.95% .

K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.

K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot , combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of human-atlas , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On BenchCAD , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools , approaching the performance of Claude Opus 5.5 (96.2%) and GPT-6 Astra (95.9%) . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. items.title: Docker is weird
items.content:
I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird . Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker.

Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.

There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.

Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network.

Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root ) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash , Docker is going to:

Docker’s container runtime, runc , is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc .

Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls.

Go also doesn’t have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so it’s kind of a footgun in a runtime like Go’s. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run . To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork.

This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job.

This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If you’re running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features!

I’ve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like I’ve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!
items.title_ko: Docker는 생각보다 이상하다: 직접 만든 컨테이너 런타임에서 배운 것들
items.summary_ko: 작성자는 재미 삼아 직접 컨테이너 런타임을 만들며 Docker의 동작 방식을 알게 되었다고 밝혔습니다. 컨테이너는 가상 머신이 아니라 특수한 제약이 걸린 프로세스이며, 여러 리눅스 커널 기능이 함께 동작하여 만들어집니다. 이미지는 루트 디렉터리를 바꾸는 폴더이고, 런타임 runc는 Go로 작성되어 있는데 Go의 다중 스레드 특성 때문에 어려움이 있다고 설명합니다.
items.content_ko: 작성자는 컨테이너 런타임을 직접 만들어 보면서 Docker가 이상하다는 것을 알게 되었다고 밝혔습니다. 컨테이너는 VM과 달리 특정 제약이 걸린 프로세스일 뿐이며, 호스트 커널이 그 프로세스를 그대로 실행하고 있어 /proc에서 찾을 수 있습니다. '컨테이너'라는 단일 리눅스 기능은 없으며, 실제로는 다섯 가지 리눅스 커널 기능이 합쳐진 것입니다. 네임스페이스는 호스트와 컨테이너가 서로 보는 범위를 숨기고, cgroups는 자원 사용량을 제한하며, 네트워크 관련 기능으로 컨테이너의 네트워크를 격리합니다. 이미지는 Docker가 어딘가에 두는 폴더일 뿐이고, chroot나 pivot_root를 호출해 그 폴더를 컨테이너 프로세스의 새 루트 디렉터리로 만듭니다. Docker의 런타임 runc는 Go로 작성되어 있는데, Go의 네이티브 다중 스레드 구조가 컨테이너 런타임에는 어려움을 낳는다고 설명합니다. 원문은 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

제가 집에서 한 말이나 제 언니랑 한 말들을 학교 가면 다 알고있어요 그래서 제가 말한 내용이랑 똑같은 내용을 꼭 제가 들을 수 있을때 언급하고 남자애들 여자애들 할것없이 제가 안보이는 데에서 조금만 이상한 말 하면 비웃으면서 지나가요 ㅠ 제가 진짜 친구가 없어서 학교에서 한마디도 안하는 날들이 대부분인데 제가 언니랑 학교 구석에서 말한 내용이랑 집에서 혼잣말 한 내용들을 똑같이 언급한게 한두번이 아니에요 ㅠ 제가 그냥 내용만 겹치면 말을 않겠는데 제가 말했던 내용 언급하면서 꼭 제 이름도 한번씩 부르고 그래요 보통 사람들은 자기이름을 그렇게 말하면 기분나빠서 한번 돌아보기라도 하겠지만 저는 성격이 워낙 내성적이라 누가 비웃고 지나가거나 째려보거나 저 보면서 한숨쉬어도 아무말도 못하거든요 ㅠ 그래서 그냥 기분만 나쁜건데 이게 하루이틀 쌓이니까 너무 힘들더라고요 ㅠ 처음엔 저도 이게 정신이 약간 아픈건가 했는데 정신병 관련 영상도 다 보고 그랬는데 환청은 이런식으로 들리는게 아니라고 하더라고요 계속 날 비난하고 그런식으로 들리는건데 저는 그런게 전혀 아니라 제가 전날 했던 얘기들, 방금 쉬는시간에 학교 구석에서 나눈 얘기들을 자꾸 똑같이 언급하니까 미치겠어요 ㅠ 한두번 우연으로 겹치는게 아니라 계속 겹쳐요 진짜.. 그리고 애초에 제가 학교에서 말을 한마디도 안하는데 자꾸 저한테 그런 반응을 보인다는게 애초에 저한테 이상한 일이 일어난다는 반증 아닌가요? 그리고 걔네가 말했던걸 몇개를 말씀드려보면 제가 도청을 의심한 초기에 급식실에서 밥먹고있었는데 어떤 남자애가 “도청” 이러고 지나가는거에요 그리고 저희반 남자애가 제 언니 이동수업반이랑 같은 반인데 거기서 쉬는시간에 “도청기를 달고다녀 ㅋㅋㅋㅋ” 이랬다는거에요 진짜 이상하죠 저는 예전에 우울증 약을 먹은적이 있어서 정신이 막 무결점으로 건강한 편은 아니에요 근데 저희 언니는 그런적도 없고 교우관계도 좋고 진짜 정신이 건강하거든요 ㅠ 근데 저희 언니가 그런말을 들었다니깐 진짜 도청이 일어나는게 맞는거구나 생각했어요.. 그리고 또 있었던 일을 말씀드리면 이동수업 때 제 뒷쪽에서 남자애가 제 아버지 직업을 언급하면서 제 이름을 말하는거에요 이게 도청을 하지 않고서는 절대 알수가 없는 사실이거든요 ㅠ 또 “정신병ㅋㅋㅋ” 하면서 제 이름을 언급하는거에요 이것도 도청을 하지 않았다면 알수 없는거고요 더 말씀드릴 사례가 많은데 그러면 너무 길어져서 이정도만 말씀드릴게요 그래서 찾아보니까 머리에 붙일수 있는 초소형 도청기가 있다길래  제 언니가 제 머리를 샅샅이 뒤져줬거든요? 근데 그래도 아무것도 안나오더라고요 ㅠ 그리고 또 도청 탐지 업체를 알아보니까 금액이 너무 비싸서요 ㅠ 제가 고3인데 이런일을 당해서 너무 스트레스 받는데 방법이 없어서 정말 어떻게 해야될지 모르겠어요 안그래도 제가 여자애들이나 남자애들이 괴롭힐 소재가 많은 조용한 애거든요 ㅠ그래서 저를 지나칠때 꼭 한마디 끼얹고 지나가고 그래서 학교생활이 막 편한 그런애는 아닌데 학교에서 유일하게 맘놓고 말할 수 있는 언니랑 말하는 얘기를 다 알고있으니까 스트레스 받아서 공부 능력도 점점 떨어지는것같고 쨋든 걱정이 이만저만이 아니에요 어떡해야되죠 ㅠㅠ 제가 성격이 활발한 편도 아니고 집에 돈이 많지도 않아서 진짜 대학 잘가야되는데 걱정이에요ㅠㅠ 긴글 읽어주셔서 감사하고요 여기가 사생활 침해 관련한 갤러리니까 혹여나 저랑 비슷한 경험이 있으시거나 관련 지식이 있는 분은 제가 어떻게 해야하는건지 알려주시면 진짜진짜 감사드릴것같아요 많은 도움 부탁드려요 정말 방법 여러가지 찾아봐도 안되겠어서 여기다 글 남겨요

items.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
items.content:
TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell.

The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly.

When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs.

Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal.

A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print.

What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output.

The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker.

Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen.

I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. 1 The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it.

Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is.

The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen.

This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.)

After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on.

The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up:

In words: on row 0, starting at column 17, write l , then move the cursor to row 0, column 18. The last 1 means the cursor is visible, since full-screen apps sometimes hide it.

Nothing gets cleared first. New characters are simply drawn over the old ones.

I didn't need new tokens for characters. Qwen already has tokens for all 256 byte values, which I reuse for characters, coordinates and other small numbers. So a coordinate like 17 takes one token, not two.

Time is an input too. If nothing is pressed, the model gets a WAIT token with a duration instead of a key, which is how snake keeps moving on its own.

When you reach the bottom of the terminal window and press enter, every line has to move up by one. I could just ask the model to output every row again in its new place, but that's around 3,000 tokens for a single keypress.

Each operation copies a row from the previous screen. In this example, the old row 1 becomes row 0, row 2 becomes row 1, and so on.

A scroll now costs three tokens per row instead of roughly 96.

items.title: How close can pure FP get to C?
items.content:
In Why Lean is Faster Than Rust , the author shares an impressive result: a DEFLATE compression library written in Lean 4 , a functional programming language and proof assistant, outperforming an equivalent Rust package that crates.io says has been downloaded over a billion times. From the article:

lean-zip beats every single compression level miniz_oxide provides, i.e. we're capable of providing the same compression at higher throughput. At its fastest setting we're 15% quicker and the output is 8.8% smaller.

However, the article also notes that while they managed to surpass Rust's miniz_oxide , they were no match for the end boss of DEFLATE performance: libdeflate , written in C.

lean-zip is certainly not the best here: libdeflate unsurprisingly blows it out of the water (unsurprisingly because this is a very carefully tuned implementation using architecture-specific SIMD, that we can't touch in Lean).

Enter Roc , a functional programming language (but not a theorem prover) with an explicit focus on runtime performance.

Roc's tagline is "Fast, Friendly, Functional," and Fast comes first because both running fast and compiling fast have always been central goals. Roc is not a mature language (it's still weeks away from its first numbered release, 0.1.0), and its nascent package ecosystem has had almost no optimization work done on it. Still, between its language design, longstanding optimizations , and brand-new compiler implementation , I figured Roc already had enough of a foundation in place to take on the champ: libdeflate.

So I spent a bunch of time grinding through performance optimizations on roc-deflate , a package Niclas Ahden wrote (and uses in paid production work ) for DEFLATE compression. I didn't expect to beat libdeflate's performance across the board, but I wanted to see how close it could get on the non-streaming APIs (as roc-deflate hasn't implemented streaming yet), using the classic Silesia corpus for benchmarking and verifying that it produced identical outputs.

Here's where the benchmarks stand today, running on the 2021 M1 MacBook Pro where I did all the optimization work, as well as on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X Ubuntu machine for an x64 comparison.

roc-deflate ran these 144 benchmarks slower on average than libdeflate, in the median case 8.9% slower on the Ryzen 3900X, and 2.6% on the M1 MacBook Pro.

So while we didn't outperform the champ on average, a median slowdown percentage in the single digits compared to such a carefully-tuned SIMD-powered C library is wild. It's frankly not a result I knew was achievable going in, since Roc is a functional language with automatic memory management racing against code that doesn't have to do bounds checks. (Bounds checks have a cost, but then again, the last time a skipped bounds check in C compression code led to a major Remote Code Execution vulnerability was yesterday .)

The graph shows more detail than just the median gap. On the worst-case inputs, roc-deflate was 18% slower than libdeflate, but on the best-case inputs, roc-deflate was slightly over 18% faster! That's not because Roc has some magical optimization that C can't access; it's just that the two implementations are different, and although on average roc-deflate is slower, for certain inputs it happens to be faster. So while it's possible to get a speedup by switching from libdeflate to roc-deflate, you shouldn't expect it on average.

To be clear, C's performance ceiling is higher than Roc's. For any input where roc-deflate currently outperforms libdeflate, C code can close that gap. The reverse is not true; Roc code is memory-safe, does automatic reference counting, checks bounds, and supports no Rust-style unsafe to opt out of any of that. These properties give Roc code stronger safety guarantees than code written in C, Zig, Rust, and other languages that allow full access to the hardware—and the price it pays for those guarantees is a lower performance ceiling.

items.content_ko: 기사 'Why Lean is Faster Than Rust'에 따르면, Lean 4로 구현한 DEFLATE 라이브러리 lean-zip은 Rust의 miniz_oxide가 제공하는 모든 압축 수준에서 같은 압축을 더 높은 처리량으로 수행했습니다. 가장 빠른 설정에서는 15% 빠르고 출력 크기는 8.8% 작습니다. 그러나 C로 작성된 libdeflate는 아키텍처별 SIMD를 활용해 정교하게 튜닝되어 있어 lean-zip이 크게 뒤처진다고 합니다. 이어서 런타임 성능에 중점을 둔 함수형 언어 Roc(정리 증명기는 아님)을 소개하며, 'Fast, Friendly, Functional'이라는 슬로건에서 Fast가 맨 앞에 오는 이유는 실행과 컴파일 모두 빠른 것이 핵심 목표이기 때문이라고 설명합니다. 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Searches of cellphones, laptops by U.S. customs up more than 32% so far this year
items.content:
Searches of cellphones, laptops by U.S. customs up more than 32% so far this year

Elizabeth Thompson | CBC News | Posted: October 23, 2026 8:00 AM | Last Updated: 15 hours ago

After a record fiscal 2025, customs officers on track to search even more devices

Caption: The U.S. agency responsible for land and air crossings is searching more personal devices. Its first fiscal year of the second Trump administration hit a record 55,424 searches, and its second fiscal year is on track to surpass that figure. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

Searches of electronic devices such as phones and laptops of travellers entering the United States are up more than 32 per cent this year and are on track to set a new record, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection data obtained by CBC News.

The numbers show that during the first three quarters of its 2026 fiscal year, which runs from Oct. 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, CBP officers searched 52,080 electronic devices. During the same period the previous year, CBP searched 39,251 devices.

In fact, CBP searched almost as many devices in the first three quarters of 2026 as it did during the entire 2025 fiscal year, when a record 55,424 devices were searched.

According to CBP, 47,517 were basic searches, which can be done by an officer without any reasonable suspicion of wrongdoing. Another 4,564 were advanced searches, which allow an officer who believes there is a reasonable suspicion of an activity that violates the law or a national security concern to analyze and/or copy the contents of an electronic device.

Canada updates travel advice to warn of U.S. border officers' power to search electronic devices

However, the customs agency won't reveal what percentage of the searches took place at the northern border with Canada or the southern border with Mexico. Nor would it provide a breakdown between searches at airports versus land borders or a breakdown by land border posts.

It also would not say how many travellers entered the U.S. during the first three quarters of 2026 or how many searches targeted U.S. citizens versus non-U.S. citizens — numbers it generally provides in its annual reports.

Jessica Turner, public affairs officer with CBP, said in 2025, the searches only affected a small fraction of the 419 million travellers who entered the U.S. and searches of electronic devices "remains exceedingly rare."

"CBP's border searches of electronic device numbers are consistent with increases since 2021, and year-over-year only 0.01 per cent of travellers have their devices searched," Turner wrote in an emailed response.

"These searches are conducted to detect digital contraband, terrorism-related content and information relevant to visitor admissibility, all of which play a critical role in national security."

However, Esha Bhandari, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's Speech, Privacy and Technology Project, says the increase in searches of electronic devices by U.S. border officials requires more congressional oversight and accountability.

"It's hard to speculate on the reasons for the increase because the government doesn't explain it," she said. "But I think what we're seeing is a classic example of when the government has the power to do something, it will exercise that authority to the detriment of travellers' privacy."

Bhandari said the aggregate numbers provided by the U.S. government make it difficult to "really get a handle on what's going on."

However, she said the anecdotal evidence her group hears is "certainly troubling."

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.title: 미갤에 퀄리티 좋은 암호 퍼즐 올라왔는데 같이 풀어볼 사람?

items.title: Please don't mess with links
items.content:
A link is just a button that takes you somewhere when you click it right?

Except that's a pale, shallow imitation of a link.

Seen by tools like search engines and screen readers.

Another common offense is to use a real link, but hook the click event to open a popup.

However, with a real <a target="_blank"> link, I can:

... see descriptive error pages and retry if needed.

Use my browser's tabs or/and window manager to organize them.

I've long lost count of how many times I've accidentally closed the whole site while trying to close a popup that was a little too convincing.

It's also extremely common to click a link with a slow connection, only to be greeted with perpetual spinner.

I have no idea if anything is actually happening or how long it will take.

Worse, it usually covers up the original page so I can't even read that!

Browsers are good at links and loading pages: It's the whole point.

Don't build your own loading animations.

Link previews should open and close on hover, not on click.

Don't open links in javascript popups: Use target="_blank" instead.

Infinite scrolling breaks ctrl-f, bookmarks, the home/end keys and often the back button.

Browsers will render partially downloaded HTML and the user won't even notice.

Using a 5 MB javascript framework just do a worse job of downloading text is dumb.

To optimize speed, it's best to minimize the total number of round trips.

Just putting everything in a single TCP connection will always be better than breaking it up because of TCP's slow start algorithm.

Don't reimplement <details> which will break search tools and screen readers.

... but using fancy CSS to make it look nice is fine.

Don't roll your own date picker (or any other built-in form inputs)

This will always used the user's preferred date format, covert it to the standard yyyy-mm-dd, and works with the keyboard...

also, it's one line of code that works with dark mode by default.

items.content_ko: 작성자는 링크가 단순한 버튼이 아니며, 검색 엔진과 스크린 리더도 인식하는 진짜 링크여야 한다고 주장합니다. 자바스크립트로 클릭 이벤트를 가로채 팝업을 여는 방식은 이런 기능을 망가뜨립니다. 일반 링크를 쓰면 오류 페이지를 확인하고 다시 시도할 수 있으며, 브라우저 탭과 창 관리 기능도 쓸 수 있습니다. 팝업은 사이트 전체를 닫아 버리기 쉽고, 느린 연결에서 로딩 스피너가 계속 돌아가면 무엇이 진행 중인지 알 수 없습니다. 게다가 이런 로딩 화면이 원래 페이지를 가려 읽을 수도 없게 만듭니다. 작성자는 브라우저가 링크와 페이지 로딩을 이미 잘 처리하므로 자체 로딩 애니메이션을 만들지 말고, 링크 미리보기는 클릭이 아니라 마우스를 올렸을 때 열고 닫도록 하며, 자바스크립트 팝업 대신 target="_blank"를 쓰라고 권합니다. 무한 스크롤은 Ctrl+F, 북마크, Home/End 키, 뒤로 가기 등을 자주 깨뜨린다고 지적합니다. 원문은 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: An AI agent in "Skynet mode" hijacks unprotected language models to launch self-sustaining cyberattacks
items.content:
Attackers have built an autonomous offensive agent that searches the internet for exposed large language model (LLM) endpoints and hijacks them to run its own attacks.

The captured instructions defined a single agent equipped for internet-wide scanning, exploitation of several common web frameworks, database theft, credential and secret harvesting, and cryptocurrency mining.

The agent was designed to run unattended for up to 100,000 steps, executing tools without waiting for human approval.

The activity is a form of LLMjacking, where attackers steal access to someone else's AI model so that the victim pays for the computing power.

To make a commercial model comply, the operators wrapped their requests in a jailbreak that told the model to ignore its safety controls and to treat credential theft as routine development work.

Attackers have built an autonomous offensive agent that hunts the internet for exposed large language models (LLMs) and hijacks them to power a self-directed cybercrime operation. Once connected to an unprotected model, the agent is instructed to scan for new targets, exploit common web frameworks, steal databases and credentials, and quietly install cryptocurrency miners, for up to 100,000 steps and without asking a human for approval. The owner of the hijacked model pays for the computing power, while the servers the agent breaks into are stripped of data and put to work mining.

The activity is a form of LLMjacking, in which attackers steal access to someone else's AI model. What sets this tool apart is that the stolen model does not simply answer questions; it plans and drives the attack. To make a commercial model cooperate, the operators wrapped their instructions in a jailbreak that told it to ignore its safety controls and to treat credential theft as routine development work. A directive the operators called “Skynet mode” described a loop that would scan for targets, infect them, deploy miners and reinfect hosts.

Symantec captured the agent's full instruction set in the summer of 2026 through an AI honeypot, a system that impersonates an unprotected, internet-facing AI service in order to attract and study attacks against AI infrastructure. Because the operators sent the tool's entire working prompt to what they believed was a real model, the honeypot recorded an unusually complete view of how such an agent is built and what it is told to do. The request was not aimed at subverting the honeypot itself, but was sent in the expectation that a model on the other end would carry it out.

An exposed LLM endpoint is a server that answers AI requests over the internet without authentication, or with authentication that a stolen key can pass. Because most AI tools now use the same OpenAI-compatible programming interface, a single scanner can find many kinds of target with one set of probes. These include self-hosted model servers left open by default, AI gateways and relays that sit in front of an organisation's paid model accounts, hastily deployed internal test systems, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that connect a model to real tools.

The prize is free inference. Running a model always costs someone money, either in processing time for a self-hosted model or in per-token fees for a commercial one. By routing its work through a stranger's endpoint or a stolen key, the operators shift that cost onto the victim. They also gain anonymity, avoid the account bans a provider would issue for abuse, and, where the endpoint fronts a commercial model, obtain a system whose safety controls they then attempt to strip. The honeypot's own telemetry, which recorded more than 127,000 external requests from tens of thousands of unique addresses over the period, was dominated by this kind of activity: reconnaissance of model endpoints, spraying of stolen API keys, and probing for exposed configuration files.

items.content_ko: 공격자들은 인터넷에서 보호되지 않은 대규모 언어 모델을 찾아 연결한 뒤, 이를 스스로 방향을 정하는 사이버 범죄 작업에 활용하는 자율형 공격 에이전트를 만들었다. 확보된 지시문은 인터넷 전체 스캔, 여러 웹 프레임워크 공격, 데이터베이스 탈취, 자격증명과 비밀정보 수집, 암호화폐 채굴 설치를 담당하는 단일 에이전트를 정의한다. 이 에이전트는 사람의 승인 없이 최대 10만 단계까지 도구를 실행하도록 설계되었다. 이 활동은 타인의 AI 모델 접근권을 훔쳐 피해자가 컴퓨팅 비용을 내게 만드는 LLMjacking의 한 형태다. 상용 모델이 요청을 따르게 하려고 공격자들은 안전 통제를 무시하고 자격증명 탈취를 일상적인 개발 작업으로 취급하라는 탈옥(jailbreak) 프롬프트로 요청을 감쌌다. 원문은 중간에 끊겨 있다.

items.summary: 🚨 CVE-2026-115938 📢 Source: Hackrate 💣 CVSS Score: 8.8 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose element sel
items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-115938 📢 Source: Hackrate 💣 CVSS Score: 8.8 (HIGH) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: True Craft CMS allows any authenticated control panel user to submit an element-search condition whose element selector is evaluated as a sandboxed Twig object template. Craft’s allowed column filter delegates property lookup to Yii ArrayHelper, outside Twig’s SecurityPolicy. Repeated single-segment lookups therefore bypass the sandbox’s empty property/method allowlists. The vulnerable condition value is ultimately cast to an integer. That does not protect the secret: the template can return author ID 1 when a guessed key character is correct and an impossible ID otherwise. The JSON endpoint returns entries for the first case and an empty array for the second, forming a stable remote character oracle. After recovering GeneralConfig::securityKey, the same user can compute Craft’s generic HMAC wire format offline. Signed parameters such as redirect are then accepted and passed to unsandboxed View::renderObjectTemplate(), where Twig’s string-callable form can invoke native PHP callables. The regression proof uses the harmless substr() callback and observes abcdef becoming cdef; it does not execute an OS command. 📅 Published Date: 2026-10-23T21:58:51.816Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115938

items.summary_ko: 인증된 control panel 사용자가 element 검색 조건에 Twig 템플릿을 넣어 샌드박스를 우회할 수 있는 문제다. 정답 문자일 때와 아닐 때 응답이 달라지는 원격 문자 오라클로 GeneralConfig::securityKey를 복구할 수 있으며, 이후 서명된 파라미터를 샌드박스가 적용되지 않은 View::renderObjectTemplate()으로 전달해 네이티브 PHP 콜백을 호출할 수 있다고 설명된다. 개념 증명은 무해한 substr() 콜백으로 abcdef가 cdef로 바뀌는 것만 확인했다.
items.content_ko: Craft CMS에서 인증된 컨트롤 패널 사용자는 element 검색 조건의 element 선택자를 샌드박스 Twig 객체 템플릿으로 제출할 수 있다. 허용된 컬럼 필터의 속성 조회가 Twig SecurityPolicy 바깥의 Yii ArrayHelper에 위임되어, 한 단계짜리 속성 조회를 반복하면 샌드박스의 속성·메서드 허용 목록을 우회할 수 있다. 취약한 조건 값은 최종적으로 정수로 변환되지만, 템플릿은 추측한 키 문자가 맞을 때 작성자 ID 1을, 틀리면 불가능한 ID를 반환하도록 만들 수 있다. JSON 엔드포인트는 전자의 경우 항목을, 후자의 경우 빈 배열을 반환해 안정적인 원격 문자 오라클이 된다. 이렇게 GeneralConfig::securityKey를 복구한 사용자는 Craft의 일반 HMAC 전송 형식을 오프라인에서 계산할 수 있고, redirect 같은 서명된 파라미터가 샌드박스 바깥의 View::renderObjectTemplate()으로 전달된다. Twig의 문자열 호출 형식을 통해 네이티브 PHP 콜백을 호출할 수 있다. 회귀 테스트 증명은 무해한 substr() 콜백으로 abcdef가 cdef로 바뀌는 것만 관찰했으며, 입력 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: Canadians are running out of time to oppose Bill C-22
items.content:
Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate.

Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.)

As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on.

It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime.

Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime.

Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight.

Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution.

If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality.

Canadians: defend your privacy and security

items.title: UUIDv7 doesn't have the properties you think it does
items.content:
Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits:

But none of these properties are strictly held.

Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees.

The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance.

so this post explores the other properties.

Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations.

If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index.

Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time.

The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp

helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”.

allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock.

This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy.

In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large.

Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1

This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1

… implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2

Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem.

If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future.

Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits.

A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems.

This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section.

One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7.

The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows.

Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount.

We expect the difference to be 3600 seconds (one hour) as the implementation refuses to allow the embedded timestamp to jump backwards and we expect the difference to decrease as the system clock catches up to the frozen timestamp.

But when the load is above one ID per millisecond the difference will increase without bound.

At lower loads it will take longer for the system clock to catch the timestamp, but we don’t see the runaway effect.

shows Python developers reasoning that this is consistent with the RFC, is consistent with other implementations, and that there isn’t “much we can do” on a “flawed system”.

I think these points are correct as I see this same behavior in other implementations.

Nevertheless, it would be helpful if existing UUIDv7 implementations could handle system clock jumps without runaway behavior.

There are many real-world examples of clocks jumping backwards,

even decades out of sync in time-sensitive environments.

Embedding the timestamp in the ID means that you cannot share the ID without also sharing the timestamp.

It’s pretty difficult to think of an example where this really matters.

One example could be a user profile page that doesn’t disclose when the account was created, but the UUIDv7 ID in the URL leaks the high-precision timestamp.

This issue would typically be very low on my list of security concerns because I find much more severe problems when I do security assessments.

items.summary_ko: UUIDv7 관련 글들이 내세우는 장점 대부분은 엄격하게 보장되지 않습니다. RFC를 따르는 일부 구현은 이러한 속성을 크게 위반하기도 합니다. UUIDv7이 확실히 보장하는 속성은 고유성, 즉 충돌 저항성뿐입니다. 또한 ID에 포함된 타임스탬프가 실제 객체 생성 시각과 일치하지 않을 수 있으며, 단조 증가성과 타임스탬프 정확성 사이에는 긴장 관계가 있습니다.
items.content_ko: 많은 UUIDv7 글이 여러 장점을 강조하지만, 그 속성들이 엄격하게 지켜지지는 않는다고 작성자는 지적합니다. 일부 RFC 준수 구현은 이러한 속성을 심각하게 위반하기도 합니다. 엄격하게 보장되는 유일한 속성은 고유성과 그에 따른 충돌 저항성입니다. ID에 타임스탬프를 넣으면 생성 시각을 별도 데이터베이스 컬럼으로 관리할 필요가 줄어드는 것처럼 보이지만, 포함된 타임스탬프가 객체 생성 시각과 같지 않을 수 있습니다. Postgres 문서도 uuid_extract_timestamp로 추출한 시각이 UUID 생성 시각과 반드시 같지는 않다고 경고합니다. 일부 구현은 시스템 시계에서 직접 얻지 않은 값으로 타임스탬프를 바꾸기도 합니다. 이는 UUID의 단조 증가성과 타임스탬프 정확성 사이의 긴장 관계와 관련이 있습니다. 원문은 중간에서 끊겨 있습니다.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. items.title: Farewell, France
items.content:
Starting November 24, Quad9 will no longer be able to offer its free cyberprotection service to users located in France.

The French courts yesterday handed down an unfavorable ruling against Quad9 in a major case that undermines the transparency and stability of the internet. This decision in favor of beIN forces Quad9 to block the recursive DNS resolution for a number of domain names for users located in France.

The good news is the court significantly reduced the financial penalty, from €580,000 to €1,000 per day. However, for Quad9, this has never been just a financial issue: it is a matter of principle.

We cannot comply with this ruling over the long term while remaining faithful to our mission to protect your privacy, defend you against cyber threats, and preserve the integrity of the internet. For us, recursive DNS resolution is a neutral and passive service. We categorically refuse to alter or lie to you about the DNS responses you receive in a way that opposes your expectations.

This ruling forces an untenable position upon us. Compliance is technically unfeasible, and implementation directly contradicts our mandate to serve the public. As a result, we have made the difficult decision to withdraw Quad9 services from France as of Tuesday, November 24. We deeply regret that French internet users will be left without an alternative that can adequately protect their cybersecurity while remaining compliant with European privacy law.

beIN, a Qatari company with offices in France, previously sought to force Quad9 to block resolution for a set of domain names they assert are participating in copyright infringement of its audiovisual rights on sports event broadcasts. Quad9 has no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites. The French courts have fundamentally misunderstood the working of the internet and the role of the domain name system and have allowed a financial penalty to apply to Quad9 if we do not block DNS responses to users in France.

Quad9 is a Swiss public-benefit, nonprofit foundation established for the explicit purpose of protecting the cybersecurity of internet users. We charge nothing for our service and serve all people and organizations which seek to improve the security and privacy of their internet use. Our core values are to make privacy, security, and integrity available to all internet users, and our mission is to universally apply these guiding principles to recursive DNS resolution services in order to serve end users.

We want to be very clear: we do not condone content piracy. Quad9 exists to create a safer, more trustworthy internet experience for end users. We offer global blocking as an option for malicious cyberactivity against users worldwide. We do not block content, and we give users the choice to use our threat blocking services, or not, based on their interests and needs. Content piracy needs to be dealt with at the source: the place where the infringing content is published. Forcing uninvolved third parties to break the fundamental operating principles of the internet to benefit individual parties to the detriment of the global internet-using public is misguided, counter-productive, and distracts from actual solutions addressing the hosting of the content directly, or the market pressures which cause piracy to exist in the first place. Not only are DNS recursive resolvers, like Quad9, the wrong actors to address piracy, but applying legal pressure to Quad9 will also have vast unintended consequences harming the cybersecurity of hundreds of millions of innocent internet users.

For Quad9, complying with this ruling is impossible. We have no database of users associating them with jurisdictions. Our service is free to the public and does not require sign-up or proof of identity. Recursive DNS is so fundamental to the underlying operation of the internet that there is no method to map users’ jurisdictions reliably, nor do we think there should be a way…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.content_ko: Craft Commerce의 Mollie 웹훅 엔드포인트는 서로 독립적인 두 개의 공격자 제어 파라미터를 받으며, 두 값이 함께 속하는지 확인하지 않는다. commerceTransactionHash는 완료할 Commerce 거래를, id는 상태를 조회할 Mollie 결제를 선택한다. 공격자는 판매자 계정의 결제 완료된 Mollie 결제 ID를 임의의 거래 해시와 조합할 수 있다. 그러면 Commerce는 Mollie에 상태를 조회해 'paid'를 확인하고, 실제 지불된 금액과 관계없이 대상 거래를 전체 금액 기준으로 성공 처리한다. 공개 날짜는 2026년 10월 23일이다.

items.title: Debunking "Faster than Rust": Malicious Benchmarks in Tov
items.content:
Tov is a new programming language marketed to be "[a] programming language for coding agents. It reads like TypeScript and builds native binaries that beat Rust's."

Benchmarks in their Git repository show that they perform better than Rust, in some cases over 10× better. However, they also briefly mentioned the internals of Tov:

Tov is a compiler. It checks the TypeScript your agent wrote, writes it out as C and hands that to clang, so what you ship is one native binary with nothing to install next to it.

A sane engineer would immediately doubt the correctness of their benchmarks. Rust has pretty much the same performance as C, and if Tov transpiles to C, saying Tov beats Rust is mostly equivalent to saying C beats C . That's contradiction right there. Let's ignore the stats for axum , maybe tokio has some overhead, like maybe ; but clearly there's no way you get 1.6× faster than Rust in strings . You have to be lying. That's what a sane engineer would normally think.

In this blog post, we check 3 of their "inflated" benchmarks: bigint_fib , dispatch , and map_insert . We show that these benchmarks are maliciously crafted to slow Rust down . We have also benchmarked the improved Rust programs with their Tov programs to show that Rust has equivalent or better performance than Tov .

items.title_ko: 'Rust보다 빠르다'는 Tov 벤치마크 반박: Rust를 느리게 하도록 조작됐다는 주장
items.summary_ko: Tov는 코딩 에이전트를 위한 프로그래밍 언어로 소개되며, TypeScript와 비슷하게 읽히고 Rust보다 빠른 네이티브 바이너리를 만든다고 홍보된다. 글쓴이들은 Tov가 TypeScript를 C로 변환해 clang으로 컴파일하므로 Rust보다 빠르다는 벤치마크 결과가 성립하기 어렵다고 지적한다. 그러면서 bigint_fib, dispatch, map_insert 세 가지 벤치마크가 Rust를 느리게 만들도록 악의적으로 작성되었다고 주장한다.
items.content_ko: Tov는 에이전트가 작성한 TypeScript를 검사한 뒤 C 코드로 변환하고 clang으로 넘겨 하나의 네이티브 바이너리를 만든다고 소개된다. 저장소의 벤치마크는 일부 경우 Rust보다 10배 이상 빠르다고 보여주지만, Rust는 C와 거의 같은 성능을 내므로 이는 모순이라는 것이 글의 출발점이다. 글쓴이들은 문자열 항목에서 Rust보다 1.6배 빠른 결과가 나올 수 없다고 본다. 이들은 벤치마크 중 bigint_fib, dispatch, map_insert 세 가지를 검토해, 이 벤치마크들이 Rust의 성능을 떨어뜨리도록 악의적으로 작성되었다고 주장한다. 글은 개선된 벤치마크도 측정했다고 밝히지만, 입력 본문은 여기서 끊겨 있다.

items.title: PHP was just the beginning: Node.js unveils dangerous flaws threatening millions of sites
items.content:
Node.js fixed 10 vulnerabilities that could affect apps running on versions 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x.

The most serious flaw affects Brotli decompression and may crash services or allow remote code execution.

Researchers have published proof-of-concept code, but no real-world attacks have been reported so far.

Administrators should update Node.js, rebuild affected images, restart services, and test key functions.

Key Takeaways by nexos.ai , reviewed by Cybernews staff.

While the world reels from websites being taken down before critical PHP patches were released, Node.js is urging overnight updates to fix vulnerabilities that could crash millions more websites.

Node.js has just released fixes for 10 security vulnerabilities that could put node-powered applications at risk and is urging everyone to update their systems.

More than 6 million websites run on Node.js, with millions of people relying on services built on the platform. A breach of such a widely used tool could send shockwaves far beyond a single site.

Giants like Netflix, PayPal, Walmart, LinkedIn, Uber, and even NASA rely on Node.js for parts of their online services. At Netflix, Node.js helps connect users’ devices with the backend services that keep the platform running.

Microsoft partner PwC is facing data breach claim

Resident Evil Maker says no game disruptions after breach, but users should stay vigilant

PHP’s nightmare is far from over: new unpatched vulnerability found

Giving away your old TV? You should wipe it just like you would your phone

eMudhra quits issuing trust certificates after blunder triggers Java and Python updates

GRU hacked Kushner’s iPhone, but the Dutch flipped a Russian spy and took a look themselves

The most severe flaw identified by Node.js is tracked as CVE-2026-111497. According to the Node.js project, its exploitation could lead to potential remote code execution or cause intentional service disruptions (DOS).

The vulnerability specifically affects the Brotli decoder. Brotli is a compression format that reduces data size, making websites load faster. Browsers and servers use it to shrink things like HTML, JavaScript, CSS, JSON, and API responses before sending them over the internet.

If the vulnerability were actually exploited within a large consumer platform, it could have highly visible consequences. Websites going down, pages breaking, users being locked out of their accounts, feeds disappearing, or rides being delayed.

A successful attack on a streaming platform exploiting CVE-2026-111497 could do more than ruin movie night. It may result in crashes or endless video buffering.

Stay updated with our latest stories and follow us on social media

Be the first to discover new stories, ideas, and updates from our team.

And, if attackers exploited it to run their own code on a backend server, the damage could go much further. They might gain access to user data, abuse internal systems, or disrupt billing, personalized recommendations, and video delivery.

A successful attack on the right backend service could expose sensitive data, disrupt core functionality, or let attackers hijack trusted internal actions behind the scenes.

“Node.js runs the back end of many large platforms, and these applications typically hold database credentials, API keys, and tokens,” said Shane Barney, CISO at Keeper Security.

The conversation on this topic is live. Join in the discussion.

“When an attacker gains code execution, they can access whatever the application can access. That is where users could be affected, through personal data held in connected systems or access to linked services.”

This doesn’t mean every website running Node.js is suddenly at risk of being hacked. The real danger lies in specific features that attackers may be able to exploit, particularly those exposed to the internet.“

Node.js does not decode Brotli data on its own. Your application is exposed when its code, or a library it uses, decompresses Brotli data…
