The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.”

That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content.

Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health.

“You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.”

“Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.”

If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

items.summary_ko: C/C++에서 정의되지 않은 동작(UB)이 실제로 어떤 결과를 낳는지 어셈블리 예시로 보여주는 글이다. 일부 사람들은 UB가 문제없다고 주장하지만, 널 포인터 역참조 같은 코드는 컴파일러가 예상치 못한 기계어를 생성할 수 있다. 본문은 `std::unreachable()`을 `int* ptr = nullptr; *ptr = 99;`로 바꾸면 생성되는 코드에서 99가 아닌 0이 주소 0에 기록된 뒤 잘못된 명령으로 프로그램이 종료되는 과정을 보여준다.
items.content_ko: 본문은 메모리 매핑 장치를 제어하는 가상의 코드를 예로 든다. `std::unreachable()`은 해당 지점에서 정의되지 않은 동작을 일으킨다고 정의되어 있다. 이 경우 컴파일러는 `device_command`에 42를 쓰는 어셈블리를 생성하고, 이후 명령은 실행된다고 설명한다. 널 포인터 역참조 예시도 다룬다. 사람들은 주소 0에 접근하면 보통 세그먼트 폴트가 난다고 생각하지만, 컴파일된 결과는 다르다. 주소 0에 0이 먼저 기록되고, 이후 잘못된 명령으로 프로그램이 중단된다. 99는 생성된 프로그램에 나타나지 않지만, 널 포인터 쓰기는 실제로 남는다. 저자는 이것이 디버거의 오류 메시지를 개선하기 위한 것일 수 있다고 추측한다. 마지막에는 생성된 어셈블리 예시가 몇 개 더 제시된다.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Hundreds of Protestors Descend on Meta Corporate Office Depicting Zuck as the Devil
items.content:
Meta’s corporate offices in São Paulo are the site of ongoing protests against election interference in the crucial national run-off elections in Brazil. Hundreds of protestors rallied at the company’s offices on Tuesday, carrying effigies mocking Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg as the devil incarnate, Venezuelan publication TeleSur reported .

The demonstration coincided with an order by Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court demanding that Meta release proof it was providing equitable treatment to both of Brazil’s presidential candidates.

Meta’s moderation methods came under international scrutiny earlier this month, after the company restricted over 1,000 social media accounts belonging to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who’s viewed as something like the Bernie Sanders of the Brazilian political scene. At the same time, Lula’s allies have accused Meta of artificially boosting content from the far-right contender for the office, Flávio Bolsonaro.

Outraged at the perceived election meddling, protestors descended on Meta’s offices with Zuckerberg masks, signs, and massive paper heads. One protest sign showed a scowling Zuckerberg with dollar signs over his eyes and “bilionario safado” scrawled in blood-red paint, translating roughly to “billionaire scoundrel.”

Others carried signs demanding “não se Meta,” or “Meta stay out,” putting extra public pressure behind the judicial demand.

For its part, Meta has publicly denied any wrongdoing with its handling of the Brazilian election materials, insisting that any perceived imbalance was caused by two global service outages, per the Associated Press .

Whether intentional or not, Brazil isn’t the only country whose political direction is quietly being dictated by the whims of a trillion-dollar tech corporation. Over the weekend, the Guardian reported that Meta had temporarily suspended Instagram accounts belonging to the No Kings coalition, a broad-tent liberal grouping which has been mobilizing protests and voter-registration drives across the US.

It all comes as higher-ups at Instagram admit they have no clue how to stem the tide of AI content flooding onto the app. Until Meta submits its explanation to the Superior Electoral Court, it remains to be seen how the extremely powerful media platform can simultaneously censor thousands of political accounts during a pivotal election cycle, while being powerless to stop the deluge of harmful AI slop suffocating its users.

items.title: Dessa: the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built
items.content:
We believe voice is the most natural way to interact with intelligence, so we created Dessa, the most authentic full-duplex speech model ever built. Talking with it feels like talking with a person…full of emotion, nuance, pauses, and a natural cadence.

Interacting with current voice AI can just plain suck. It turns your voice into text and throws away an incredible amount of information text alone can’t carry. The most powerful AIs in the world can’t hear how you feel. We think that’s ridiculous, leads to a worse experience, and is potentially dangerous.

We trained Dessa from scratch on nothing but human conversation. Sounds! No text, no pretrained models. It learned to hold a real-time conversation simply by listening. As far as we know, Dessa is the world’s first AI you can have a realistic live conversation with that was trained only from human speech.

Dessa advances the frontier of deep learning models and creates a different category with entirely new and interesting behaviors for researchers to discover. How efficiently do they learn language and facts compared to text? How efficiently can they learn new languages? What sorts of In-context learning can they perform?

Every clip below is a live recording of a person talking to Dessa. Nobody steers it. Dessa picks what to say, when to say it and how, down to its own voice and personality. Subtitles were added afterward.

It laughs the moment something’s funny, mid-sentence, the way people do. Other models wait for you to finish, then laugh on cue. Ask it to speak up and it gets louder. Nobody taught it that.

The person blanks on a movie title. Dessa finishes the sentence. It also knows a surprising amount, considering every fact it has come from raw sound.

A surprise. Dessa gasps “oh my god” under its breath, then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude.

In this demo, Dessa is talking with GPT-Live-1, a third-party AI model. Both voices are AI-generated. The developer of GPT-Live-1 is not affiliated with Block and has not reviewed or endorsed Dessa.

More recordings will be shared on X soon.

Audio in, audio out. Dessa is a true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech. It’s full-duplex, so it listens and talks at the same time, like you do. It learned from real conversation, so it knows when to cut in and when to backchannel (“yeah!”, “got it!”, “ooh”) to show it’s with you. Inference runs faster than real time, so there’s no awkward wait. And it runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better.

It natively hears and speaks emotion, sarcasm, laughter, a frustrated sigh, a voice cracking with sadness. Run speech through text and all of that is gone, which is why most voice AI feels stilted, slow and, worst of all, annoying.

LLMs need an insane amount of text. Dessa learned language from hundreds of times fewer words (in fairness, LLMs also have to learn C++ and whatever the hell Angular is).

And it had to learn far more than language. Accents, pauses, breathing, sarcasm, humor, inflection, emotion, when to cut in: every one changes what someone means. Say “I didn’t say she stole my CUDA code” out loud, stressing a different word each time. Same words, different meaning every time.

Speech never repeats. Say a sentence twice, exactly the same way, and the data still comes out different. Text is identical no matter who types it. And a single spoken word takes thousands of times more bytes than the same word in text. People learn to talk so easily that we forget how hard it is. For a machine with no text to lean on, it’s brutal.

But, we figured it out. And we figured out how to train Dessa on only one NVIDIA GB200 NVL72.

Three reasons: curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety.

Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.

items.title: Head of Instagram Says He Has No Idea How to Deal With Wave of Horrible AI Slop
items.content:
AI slop purveyors are stealing comedians’ jokes to create viral Instagram videos of fake comics. And Adam Mosseri, the longtime head of Instagram, says he doesn’t know what to do about it.

As Wired reported last week , a recent trend among AI sloppers is to steal the work of real comedians and repackage it in AI-manipulated clips in which the human performers are replaced by fake AI ones. The AI performers in the videos are often depicted as voluptuous young women and direct viewers to OnlyFans pages, where they’re encouraged to pay for more content.

George Brett Olson, a comedian whose work was ripped off by a thieving AI account with more than 300,000 followers, published a video earlier this month detailing how his work — and even his outfit — were stolen by the AI fake. This prompted a response from Mosseri, who commented that he doesn’t “think it’s practical for us to try and ban Al content from the platform. It’s gonna be harder and harder to identify, and it’s not all bad content (though yes, there is plenty of slop).”

“But we are very invested in trying to drive more traffic to original content creators, and if an Al creator is ripping off content wholesale, it would be good for us to work out what we can do about that,” Mosseri continued. “I’m not sure what it would be, but I’ll make sure to talk to the team and look into it.”

This past weekend, in response to a completely different type of content that was ripped off from a creator and rehashed as AI slop — in this case, a video of a visual artist’s work —  Mosseri waded into the AI ripoff trend once again, writing that it’s a “tricky problem” and Instagram is still trying to figure out what to do.

“To be clear, I am very worried about this trend. We are actively working out what to do; it’s just a tricky problem,” Mosseri wrote in a comment on Threads , again in response to Olson. “We already let people make copyright claims against content and take stolen copyrighted material.”

“That’s not enough, though, as I assume many comedians and dancers haven’t gone through the trouble to copyright their material,” he added. “We need a way to help those creatives without letting bad actors make more fake claims (happens all the time unfortunately).”

Given Meta’s stake in the AI race, it’s unlikely that the tech giant will move to rid any of its social media platforms of AI content. And to Mosseri’s point, theft and copyright infringement isn’t exactly a new problem. But while stealing someone else’s work and passing it off as your own is an old problem, AI makes it easer than ever to rip people off with basically zero effort. You no longer have to get on stage and perform a standup set to pilfer from a fellow comic, let alone record it and then post it online; to filch someone’s artwork, you don’t have to actually draw or paint. In other words, the barrier of entry is now amazingly low: all you have to do is set up an AI workflow and hit generate, and you have endless low-effort slop to pump out to the masses. (And if you’re able to convince people that you’re not a thieving sloperator and are instead a hot human woman, you might just rake in some extra cash via OnlyFans in the process.)

It’ll be interesting to see how Meta moves to combat this kind of abuse across its social media platforms, Instagram included — or if it’ll continue to be up to creators to find and report individual instances of abuse piecemeal, and at the mercy of the platform’s tepid moderation efforts.

items.title: Can we replace a $150k Looker with a bucket of HTML files?
items.content:
Like a lot of companies, we pay for Looker. Let’s say $150k a year, the average Looker licence 1 , roughly 300 seats. We are 3 data platform engineers at a company of about 500 people, and most of our week goes on the unglamorous stuff: keeping Snowflake fed, babysitting a dbt project that passed 2,000 models a while ago, and running the Airflow, Airbyte, DataHub and Kubernetes plumbing underneath it all.

In February, one of us built a thing on the side to host HTML files. It took an afternoon. 8 months later, and it’s already got as many weekly users as Looker in our company, maybe even more and Looker’s down a third.

Tech influencers keep posting about software being dead , and some say they’ve cancelled and vibecoded all their SaaS subscriptions . They say AI is going to kill B2B SaaS. 2

SaaS is dead, apparently, so can we replace our enterprise BI tool?

Left: share of new GitHub repos described as "self-hosted". Right: share of Hacker News comments saying "slop". 3

A year ago I thought most AI output was slop, and most of it was. We made a few “chat with your data” demos, and they looked great on a toy schema with 4 tables, but never really worked at our scale. The SQL ran without errors, but the numbers were wrong. That’s much worse.

Then Claude Code with Opus 4.5 got really good. Like, really good. In early January adoption across the company skyrocketed. It could work in our repos and use our tools. Also, it could run a query to check the numbers before answering. That mattered a lot more than getting a clever-sounding response. Within a few weeks, people in finance, ops and marketing who had never opened a terminal were prompting all day. All of a sudden everyone was prompting, and nobody was clicking.

Around this time, Claude started spitting out a lot of HTML. You would ask for an analysis and you’d get a single file with charts, and honestly, some of those pages looked better than our Looker dashboards. The problem was that it would live in someone’s Downloads folder. To share it, they would attach it in Slack and hope. This was way before Anthropic shipped shareable artifacts for Team and Enterprise (June 2026), and we really needed a way to share this new kind of dashboard.

We needed to host and share our HTML slop

One day Maddy from our team said she’d just put them all on a web server, with an internal domain name. By the end of the day she had vibe-coded the whole thing: a small service that stored the files in S3, SSO in front of it, and (some) tests. We already run everything on Kubernetes, so deploying a service was mostly a matter of adding a Terraform module and a Helm chart. Having all that plumbing in place made the whole thing much easier.

She wrote a small Python script and packaged it in a Claude plugin. Users would get their Claude to write the HTML, the script would push it (behind SSO), and anyone in the company could open the link. Initially, the files were just plain, static HTML. In March we thought, why not, and added a live query API using the viewer’s Snowflake OAuth token: best decision of the year.

Turns out, we didn’t need to write a permission model. Snowflake already had one all along. It had roles we’d been maintaining for years, and if Snowflake says you can’t read the sales table, then neither can the dashboard. By April, Snowflake OAuth was the only login.

People loved it, for a reason that's embarrassing for the BI industry: the dashboards actually looked good.

A Looker tile is a box with a fixed list of chart types and a fixed set of colours, and it looks like every other Looker tile ever made. Ugly, and no personality.

Free-form LLM-generated HTML in less than 1 minute

By getting rid of the rigid fixed tiles, our users could produce free-form HTML and prompt it until it looked neat. They loved it. distro, it can also be described as chroot on steroids.

When you want to run some software with some degree of isolation on a VPS,

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: A Markdown File Should Just Open
items.content:
It seems strange to me that in 2026 we still cannot open a Markdown document on just about any computer or phone and expect it to display properly without installing additional software. Markdown has been around for more than 20 years and has become an essential format for documentation, writing, publishing and sharing information. It is simple, portable, human-readable and supported by an enormous collection of applications and websites. Yet something as ordinary as receiving a .md file can still leave people staring at raw formatting syntax or looking for an application capable of displaying it as a document. We have operating systems that can open photographs, play videos, read PDFs and recognize countless complicated file formats without requiring us to think about how any of that works. I think Markdown deserves the same treatment.

I have been using Markdown for years, and it has become one of my favorite ways to write and organize information. Much of the content on my personal website begins as Markdown because it allows me to focus on writing rather than formatting. I can keep those files in Git, edit them with almost any text editor, convert them into webpages and preserve the original documents without depending on a proprietary application. There is something wonderfully reassuring about knowing that the words I write today should remain accessible decades from now, even if every application I currently use disappears. A Markdown document does not require an account, a subscription, a particular company or a complicated file format to remain useful. That simplicity is precisely why I think it should be treated as a first-class document throughout the computing world.

We have made something simple unnecessarily complicated

One of the original ideas behind Markdown was that a document should remain readable even before a computer interprets its formatting. John Gruber introduced the format in 2004 with help from Aaron Swartz, using ordinary text conventions to represent headings, links, emphasis and other common document structures. The result was a way to write structured material without surrounding every sentence with HTML tags or working inside a specialized document editor. Anyone who has opened a README file in a software repository has probably encountered Markdown, even if they did not know what the format was called. Its usefulness eventually spread far beyond programming into books, technical documentation, academic notes, publishing systems and personal knowledge collections. The format succeeded largely because it required so little from the software used to create it.

That is what makes the current situation so frustrating. Markdown is already plain text, so nearly every operating system can technically open it with some kind of text editor. The missing piece is treating the file as a document instead of merely displaying the characters used to describe its formatting. A heading should look like a heading, a table should look like a table, and a link should behave like a link. If I want to see the original Markdown syntax, I should be able to switch to that view just as easily. None of this should require finding an obscure utility, installing a preview extension or moving the document into an application that converts it into another format.

I can send someone a PDF with a reasonable expectation that their computer or phone will know what to do with it. They can usually open the file, read the contents, search for text and navigate the document without worrying about which company manufactured their device. Markdown should be at least that easy to read, especially considering how much simpler the underlying format is. Unlike PDF, Markdown is also designed to be edited directly, which makes consistent support even more valuable. items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-115895 📢 Source: GitHub_M 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False Happy DOM is a JavaScript implementation of a web browser without its graphical user interface. From 17.0.0 until 21.0.4, packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts accepts a named ESM import alias without validating that it is a JavaScript binding identifier before inserting it into a generated destructuring binding. With enableJavaScriptEvaluation enabled, attacker-controlled HTML or module source can use an invalid alias that becomes a valid default initializer after compilation, causing the generated JavaScript to execute in the Node.js host process. The demonstrated reachable path uses a JSON module import attribute, which prevents the malicious alias from being emitted again in a later ESM circular-import assignment and keeps the generated function syntactically valid. This incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33943 is a distinct residual path because the earlier remediation validated the local export importName path but not the named-import alias.
